processing: Guava leaves are dried and cut, then steeped or boiled. Methods differ by maker.
harvest_season: No prized picking season is documented; the tea sells all year.
appearance_dry: Cut, dull green to brownish leaf pieces.
appearance_wet: Soft olive-brown leaf pieces with visible veins.
taste_profile: Clean and refreshing when hot; iced, it leaves a slight bitterness in the aftertaste.

brewing.notes: Steep a bag or loose leaf for 3 to 5 minutes, to taste. If the bitterness bothers you, try it hot or blend it with another tea.

vintage_note: Sold with no vintage, as tea bags and loose cut leaf, all year.
description:
Banshirū is the Okinawan word for guava, and banshirū-cha is the local name for tea made from its leaves. It is not a fruit tea in the usual sense: there is no pulp, just the leaf of a small tropical tree, and no true tea unless someone blends it in.

The leaves are dried and usually steeped or boiled directly, and methods differ by maker.

Hot, it reads as clean and refreshing; cold, a bitter touch shows up on the finish. Keep steeps to a few minutes, and blend with another tea if it is too sharp. Remember that blending with true tea adds caffeine.

Buy it as a pleasant daily drink, not as medicine: packaging tends to run ahead of the evidence.
history: Guava leaves are said to have been steeped as tea in China long ago. In Japan the fruit is grown only in small amounts, in Okinawa and Kagoshima. Little is documented about when the tea habit started in Okinawa.
